newsitem.title: UK: Major promises low tax economy for Britain.
newsitem.headline: Major promises low tax economy for Britain.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major said on Monday his government was committed to reducing public spending to create a permanent low tax economy.

In an article in the Financial Times just three months before he must call a general election, Major outlined his government's achievements and said there would be dangers ahead if the opposition Labour Party was elected.
He said his Conservative government was on target to reduce public spending to 40 percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) and this could lead to tax cuts.
"Our commitment to reduce public spending below 40 percent of GDP and to keep it there will not only ensure sound finances. It should also enable us to find further scope for tax cuts," Major wrote.
"We privatised many loss-making nationalised industries, cut back on government subsidies, curbed growth in social-security benefits and increased the efficiency of public services," he added.
Seeking an unprecedented fifth Conservative win in the election due by the May 22, Major took a swipe at Labour which is leading the Conservatives by up to 20 points in latest opinion polls.
He said Labour, which has been in opposition for 18 years, had no objective or aim to reduce public spending as a proportion of national income.
"For all Labour's rhetoric about being tough on public spending, it remains committed to policies which could only be fulfilled by spending more," he said.

"If offers a return to European social democratic policies, policies that go hand in hand with higher levels of spending and taxation. Those policies would inevitably lead to slower economic growth and more job loseses."
Comparing Britain's performance to its European neighbours, Major said that while its public spending was going down, theirs was increasing.
"The average level of public spending in the European Union rose from 44 percent of GDP in 1979 to around 50 percent today," he said.
Major will meet senior cabinet ministers on Monday in what some newspapers claim will be a get-together to approve the party's election manfesto.
The Independent said the prime minister would be putting his house in order and clearing the decks for an election in early May.
Conservatives hoped that would allow more time for voters to reap the benefits of economic recovery so their support could be won at the election.
"It is likely that more meetings will be needed before the manifesto is finally approved, but those close to Mr Major say he has set his mind on May 1 (for the election)," the Independent said.
